EyeDiagram.Description: PRBS-modulated transient → eye persistence heat map, Q-factor and BER (shot/thermal/RIN noise).
EyeDiagram.HelpTip: What is an eye diagram? (plain-language explainer)
EyeHelp.BerBody: — the estimated bit-error rate: the chance a bit is read wrongly. 1E-12 means about one error per trillion bits (excellent); 1E-3 means the link is unusable without error correction.
EyeHelp.EyeMetricsBody: — the vertical and horizontal opening of the eye, and how much the signal edges wander in time. More opening = more margin.
EyeHelp.Intro: Signal quality at a glance: the output waveform is cut into slices, one bit long each, and all slices are drawn on top of each other. Where the 1s and 0s stay apart, an open "eye" appears in the middle.
EyeHelp.QBody: — how far apart the 1-level and 0-level sit compared to the noise. Bigger is better; Q ≈ 7 is roughly "error-free" in practice.
EyeHelp.RunBody1: It sends a pseudo-random bit stream (PRBS, like real data traffic) at the chosen bit rate through your circuit, stacks the strongest output into a brightness map (bright = the signal passes there often), and computes the quality numbers below the plot — including realistic receiver noise (shot, thermal and laser RIN).
EyeHelp.RunBody2: Light enters at couplers with the laser switched on; couplers with the laser switched off are your outputs — the eye is measured there (toggle the laser icon on the canvas or the switch in the properties panel).
EyeHelp.RunTitle: What does Run Eye Analysis do?
EyeHelp.ThresholdBody: — the decision level between 0 and 1, as a fraction of the signal range. 0.5 = exactly in the middle; move it if your 1s and 0s are asymmetric.
EyeHelp.Title: What is an eye diagram?
EyeHelp.WhyBody: A receiver must decide, in the middle of every bit, whether it sees a 1 or a 0. A wide-open eye means that decision is easy and data arrives error-free. Noise, echoes and pulse spreading squeeze the eye shut — this plot shows how much margin your circuit leaves.

Real ubcpdk (SiEPIC) and nazca-native cells are used where available; other components fall back to stub geometry. Mixed designs render each backend's part separately and merge into one GDS via two editable scripts. If gdsfactory isn't installed, it is set up in a managed environment automatically.

TransientHelp.CwBody: — light switched on and kept on. Use it to check power splitting: after a brief settling time, each output holds its share of the input power.
TransientHelp.GaussianBody: — one short flash of light. Use it to see delays and echoes: each output shows when, and how smeared-out, the flash arrives.
TransientHelp.Intro1: Think of it as an oscilloscope for your chip: light is sent into the inputs, and the plot shows how much power arrives at each output — moment by moment, not just the final steady value.
TransientHelp.Intro2: Light enters at couplers with the laser switched on; couplers with the laser switched off are your outputs (toggle the laser icon on the canvas or the switch in the properties panel).
TransientHelp.PrbsBody: — a pseudo-random stream of 0/1 data bits, like real network traffic (e.g. 25 Gbit/s). Use it to judge signal quality: are the 1s and 0s still clearly separated at the output? The same seed always produces the same bit pattern, so results are reproducible.
TransientHelp.ReadingBody: X axis: time, in picoseconds or nanoseconds (see the axis label — 1000 ps = 1 ns). Y axis: the optical power arriving at that output. Each coloured line is one output pin of your circuit; use the checkboxes under the plot to show or hide lines.
TransientHelp.ZoomNote: Zooming: hold Ctrl (Cmd on macOS) and scroll over the plot to zoom; plain scrolling moves the panel. Drag with the right mouse button to pan.
Analysis.Chart.ZoomHint: Ctrl+scroll to zoom (Cmd on macOS) · right-drag to pan · scroll to move the panel
TransientHelp.Title: What does Transient mode do?
TransientHelp.WhyBody: The normal simulation (CW mode) only shows the end state. Transient mode shows *when* light arrives, how short pulses spread out on the way, and whether fast data survives the trip through your circuit — the questions that matter for real communication links.

VerilogAExport.CaveatsBody:
Generated for the OpenVAF + NGSpice OSDI flow.

• Compile each *.va to *.osdi with OpenVAF.
• The SPICE test bench loads the OSDI artefacts via the NGSpice-specific 'pre_osdi' directive.
• Each optical port is exported as TWO electrical nodes — *_re and *_im — because Verilog-A has no native complex voltages. Driving only the real node simulates a real-valued source; driving both reproduces the photonic complex amplitude.

Other simulators (Cadence Spectre, Synopsys HSPICE, Mentor AMS) need adaptation — 'pre_osdi' is an NGSpice extension, and the twin-node model is a Lunima convention, not a Verilog-A standard.
